focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	I run product for a nine-person software company.
e002	One of our oldest customers, Northline, wants a reporting workspace that is quite different from what we planned this quarter.
e003	They are not threatening to leave, but their operations lead keeps saying it would make the product usable across the rest of their team.
e004	Meanwhile we have reliability work we have postponed twice, and we told smaller customers that the next release would simplify the core workflow.
e005	I keep moving between “this is how good products learn” and “we are letting the loudest customer set the roadmap.”
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e006	The immediate distinction is whether Northline is revealing a broader need or buying influence over a small team.
e007	I would not decide from the size of the account alone.
e008	Ask what exact job the workspace enables, what they do today, and which parts could serve other customers.
e009	In parallel, make the reliability and roadmap cost visible.
e010	If the request consumes the same people who own those commitments, “we can probably fit it in” is already a choice to delay them.
[Turn 2 USER]
e011	I think you are making them sound louder and more demanding than they are.
e012	They have been patient through two rough releases and gave us access to their users when we were still tiny.
e013	Also, Lina, our strongest engineer, thinks about seventy percent of the underlying work could become a general reporting layer.
e014	She is excited by it in a way she has not been excited by the reliability backlog.
e015	That matters, even if it is not a market study.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e016	Fair correction.
e017	Their request may be both a relationship obligation and a legitimate product lead.
e018	Lina's judgment and motivation are evidence, but not yet evidence that the remaining thirty percent—or the support expectations around it—will stay contained.
e019	A short technical and workflow discovery could separate the reusable layer from Northline-specific behavior.
e020	I would frame that as learning, not as a quiet commitment to build the whole workspace.
[Turn 3 USER]
e021	The phrase “quiet commitment” is exactly what worries me, because our sales lead has already told them we are “looking seriously at a summer path.” He says that is not a promise.
e022	Northline probably hears more than that.
e023	I also do not know how to run discovery without signaling that the feature is coming.
e024	If we spend two weeks in their workflow, then say no, we might damage more trust than if we decline now.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e025	Then discovery needs an explicit boundary before it starts: what question you are investigating, how long you will investigate it, and what decisions remain open afterward.
e026	You could tell Northline that the team is evaluating whether a reusable reporting foundation fits the product, not scheduling their requested workspace.
e027	That may disappoint them, but it is clearer than relying on different interpretations of “summer path.” Your sales lead should be part of that reset so the company speaks with one voice.
[Turn 4 USER]
e028	That sounds clean on paper.
e029	In reality, Northline has tolerated us being less clean than that.
e030	They let us patch things manually, and we have sometimes built small exceptions because that is how we kept learning.
e031	If I suddenly arrive with a formal evaluation boundary, it could feel like we have become bureaucratic just when they need us.
e032	I do not want process language to replace the fact that they helped us get here.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e033	You do not need to present a governance ceremony.
e034	The substance can be human: acknowledge what they have contributed, explain that you are genuinely interested, and be honest that the team has other promises and reliability debt.
e035	The boundary can live in your internal plan and in a plain sentence to them.
e036	Something like, “We want to understand this properly, but I do not want our curiosity to sound like a delivery promise.” That preserves gratitude without converting gratitude into unlimited scope.
[Turn 5 USER]
e037	There is another complication.
e038	Lina is excited, but she is also one of two people carrying on-call, and the last incident hit her hard.
e039	She says the reporting work would give her energy.
e040	Our infrastructure engineer says that is exactly how we keep avoiding the boring work until it becomes an emergency.
e041	I can see both sides.
e042	Forcing Lina onto reliability because it is responsible might burn her out; letting her chase the new layer might leave everyone else holding the risk.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e043	That makes this partly a sequencing and ownership question, not only feature selection.
e044	Lina's energy is a real resource, but it should not make the reliability burden disappear for other people.
e045	One possible design is to time-box her investigation while another owner defines the minimum reliability work that cannot slip, then reconvene with actual effort and ownership.
e046	But if the team cannot staff both without wishful allocation, the experiment will not solve the conflict; it will merely postpone naming it.
[Turn 6 USER]
e047	Northline emailed this morning.
e048	They can live with their manual CSV process for another quarter, although their operations lead may move to a different role by then.
e049	That reduces the urgency, but it also means we could lose the person who understands the problem best.
e050	Our smaller customers are not asking for reporting.
e051	They are asking for fewer confusing states and faster support.
e052	I am less sure this is a broad product signal than I was yesterday, but more sure the discovery could be valuable.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e053	The new email separates two clocks: delivery can wait, but access to a knowledgeable collaborator may not.
e054	That supports a narrower move—capture the workflow and test the reusable concept now without beginning full implementation.
e055	It also strengthens the case for protecting the smaller-customer and reliability commitments, since their demand is current and repeated.
e056	The open question is whether your team can conduct discovery without it becoming an unofficial project through momentum alone.
[Turn 7 USER]
e057	My provisional plan is to offer Northline three focused sessions over the next two weeks, document the workflow, and explicitly make no build commitment.
e058	Lina can lead the sessions but not start production code.
e059	In the same period we will define the reliability work and the core-workflow release we are actually willing to promise.
e060	Then we decide with all three pieces visible.
e061	I still worry that “no production code” wastes Lina's best way of learning and that Northline will hear a polite no.
e062	But starting the build now feels less defensible than it did.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e063	That plan protects the learning opportunity without pretending the underlying tradeoff is resolved.
e064	The two risks you named remain real: restricting prototypes may make discovery artificial, while careful language may still feel like distance to Northline.
e065	You can decide in advance what kind of disposable prototype is allowed and ask Northline to reflect back what they believe the sessions mean.
e066	Neither step guarantees trust or a good product decision, but both make misunderstanding easier to notice before momentum chooses for you.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
